e-9036.knowledge_point: Reducing a First-Order ODE to a Separable Form by Factoring and Using a Linear Substitution
e-9036.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}  = 2xy - x^2 - y^2.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z= x - y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form $z'(x) = f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
e-9036.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-(x-y)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z = x - y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} = 1 - \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} \quad \Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} =  1 - \dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =-{z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form $z'(x) = f(z),$ we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  =  z^2 + 1.
$$

Therefore, $f(z) = z^2 + 1.$

e-9038.knowledge_point: Solving a First-Order ODE by Factoring and Using a Linear Substitution
e-9038.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}  = \dfrac{1 - x - y}{x + y}.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y) = 2x + C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
e-9038.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1-(x+y)}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z = x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} = 1 + \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} - 1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =\frac{1-z}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form $z'(x) = f(z)$ gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{z}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}z\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int z\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ \frac{{z}^{2}}{2} & =x+K \\ {z}^{2} & =2x+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C = 2K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
(x+y)^2 = 2x + C
$$

Therefore, 

$$
g(x,y) = (x+y)^2.
$$

Using a substitution of the form z=x+y, transform the differential equation into an equation of the form z′(x)=f(z). What is the function f(z)?

content.knowledge_point: Reducing a First-Order ODE to a Separable Form by Factoring and Using a Linear Substitution
content.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=4x+4y-1.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=x+y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
content.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4(x+y)-1\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =4z-1\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=4z.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=4z.$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{8x-12y+1}{12x-18y+3}.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=2x-3y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
after.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{4(2x-3y)+1}{6(2x-3y)+3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x-3y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2-3\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}(2-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}).
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}(2-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}) & =\frac{4z+1}{6z+3}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2z+1}.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=\frac{1}{2z+1}.$

Consider the differential equation dydx=8x−12y+112x−18y+3. Using a substitution of the form z=2x−3y, transform the differential equation into an equation of the form z′(x)=f(z). What is the function f(z)?

a
4z+16z+3
b
z+12
c
z+1z+3
d
1−2z
e
12z+1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation, and we get dydx=4(2x−3y)+16(2x−3y)+3.

Then, we make the substitution z=2x−3y. Differentiating z(x) using the chain rule, we get dzdx=2−3dydx⟹dydx=13(2−dzdx). Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of z as follows: 13(2−dzdx)=4z+16z+3

Expressing this equation in the form z′(x)=f(z) gives dzdx=12z+1. Therefore, f(z)=12z+1.

content.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{8x-12y+1}{12x-18y+3}.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=2x-3y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
content.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{4(2x-3y)+1}{6(2x-3y)+3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x-3y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2-3\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}(2-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}).
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}(2-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}) & =\frac{4z+1}{6z+3}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2z+1}.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=\frac{1}{2z+1}.$

after.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{9x-3y}.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
\frac{2}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡|g(x,y)|=y+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
after.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2}{3(3x-y)}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=3x-y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=3-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=3-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2}{3z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{9z-2}{3z}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3z}{9z-2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{3z}{9z-2}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{3}\int (1+\frac{2}{9z-2})\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{3}(z+\frac{2}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡|9z-2|) & =x+K \\ z+\frac{2}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡|9z-2| & =3x+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=3K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-y+\frac{2}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡|27x-9y-2| & =3x+C \\ \frac{2}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡|27x-9y-2| & =y+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
g(x,y)=27x-9y-2.
$$

$$

$$

Consider the differential equation dydx=2tan⁡(5x+5y)−1.

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form ln⁡|g(x,y)|=10x+C, where C is a constant. What is g(x,y)?

a

b

c

EXPLANATION

First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation. dydx=2tan⁡(5(x+y))−1.

Then, we make the substitution z=x+y. Differentiating z(x) using the chain rule, we get dzdx=1+dydx⟹dydx=dzdx−1. Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of z as follows: dzdx−1=2tan⁡(5z)−1

Expressing this equation in the form z′(x)=f(z), we get dzdx=2tan⁡(5z).

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to x:

cot⁡(5z)dzdx=2∫cot⁡(5z)dz=2∫dx15ln⁡|sin⁡(5z)|=2x+Kln⁡|sin⁡(5z)|=10x+C where C=5K.

Finally, we write the equation in terms of y and x using our original substitution, as follows: ln⁡|sin⁡(5x+5y)|=10x+C Therefore, g(x,y)=sin⁡(5x+5y).

content.knowledge_point: Solving a First-Order ODE by Factoring and Using a Linear Substitution
content.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2\operatorname{tan}⁡(5x+5y)-1.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|g(x,y)|=10x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
content.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2\operatorname{tan}⁡(5(x+y))-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =2\operatorname{tan}⁡(5z)-1\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2\operatorname{tan}⁡(5z).
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cot}⁡(5z)\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =2 \\ \int \operatorname{cot}⁡(5z)\,\text{d}z & =2\int \text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡(5z)| & =2x+K \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡(5z)| & =10x+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=5K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x+5y)|=10x+C
$$

Therefore, 

$$
g(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x+5y).
$$

$$

$$
z=x+y.

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =(z+1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=(z+1)^{2}+1.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{(z+1)^{2}+1}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{(z+1)^{2}+1}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ \operatorname{arctan}⁡(z+1) & =x+C\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x+y+1)=x+C
$$

Therefore, 

$$
g(x,y)=x+y+1.
$$

Question 8

Consider the differential equation dydx=(x+y)2+2(x+y)+1.

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form arctan⁡(g(x,y))=x+C, where C is a constant. What is g(x,y)?

a
x+y
b
1(x+y)2
c
x+y+1
d
1x+y+1
e
(x+y)2−1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation. dydx=(x+y+1)2

Then, we make the substitution z=x+y. Differentiating z(x) using the chain rule, we get dzdx=1+dydx⟹dydx=dzdx−1. Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of z as follows: dzdx−1=(z+1)2

Expressing this equation in the form z′(x)=f(z) gives dzdx=(z+1)2+1.

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to x:

1(z+1)2+1dzdx=1∫1(z+1)2+1dz=∫dxarctan⁡(z+1)=x+C

Finally, we write the equation in terms of y and x using our original substitution, as follows: arctan⁡(x+y+1)=x+C Therefore, g(x,y)=x+y+1.

content.knowledge_point: Solving a First-Order ODE by Factoring and Using a Linear Substitution
content.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(x+y)^{2}+2(x+y)+1.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
\operatorname{arctan}⁡(g(x,y))=x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
content.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =(x+y+1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =(z+1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=(z+1)^{2}+1.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{(z+1)^{2}+1}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{(z+1)^{2}+1}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ \operatorname{arctan}⁡(z+1) & =x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x+y+1)=x+C
$$

Therefore, 

$$
g(x,y)=x+y+1.
$$

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2x+y}{3-2x-y}.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|g(x,y)|=-\frac{x+y}{3}+C
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
after.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2x+y}{3-(2x+y)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2+\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2 & =\frac{z}{3-z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{6-z}{3-z}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(\frac{3-z}{6-z})\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int (\frac{z-3}{z-6})\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ \int (\frac{3}{z-6}+1)\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ 3\operatorname{ln}⁡|z-6|+z & =x+K\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+y-6|+2x+y & =x+K \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+y-6| & =-\frac{x+y}{3}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=\frac{K}{3}.$

Therefore,

$$
g(x,y)=2x+y-6.
$$

Question 9
?

Consider the differential equation dydx=2x+y3−2x−y.

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form ln⁡|g(x,y)|=−x+y3+C

where C is a constant. What is g(x,y)?

a
x+y−6
b
2x+y−3
c
−x−y+3
d
2x+y−6
e
2x+y+3
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation. dydx=2x+y3−(2x+y).

Then, we make the substitution z=2x+y. Differentiating z(x) using the chain rule, we get dzdx=2+dydx⟹dydx=dzdx−2. Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of z as follows: dzdx−2=z3−z

Expressing this equation in the form z′(x)=f(z) gives dzdx=6−z3−z.

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to x:

(3−z6−z)dzdx=1∫(z−3z−6)dz=∫dx∫(3z−6+1)dz=∫dx3ln⁡|z−6|+z=x+K

Finally, we write the equation in terms of y and x using our original substitution, as follows: 3ln⁡|2x+y−6|+2x+y=x+Kln⁡|2x+y−6|=−x+y3+C, where C=K3.

Therefore, g(x,y)=2x+y−6.

verification.explanation: Setting z=2x+y gives z'=(6-z)/(3-z). Integration yields 3ln|z-6|+z=x+K, hence ln|2x+y-6|=-(x+y)/3+C. This confirms option d and agrees with the worked solution; the incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option c.

content.knowledge_point: Solving a First-Order ODE by Factoring and Using a Linear Substitution
content.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2x+y}{3-2x-y}.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|g(x,y)|=-\frac{x+y}{3}+C
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
content.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2x+y}{3-(2x+y)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2+\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2 & =\frac{z}{3-z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{6-z}{3-z}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(\frac{3-z}{6-z})\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int (\frac{z-3}{z-6})\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ \int (\frac{3}{z-6}+1)\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ 3\operatorname{ln}⁡|z-6|+z & =x+K\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+y-6|+2x+y & =x+K \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+y-6| & =-\frac{x+y}{3}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=\frac{K}{3}.$

Therefore,

$$
g(x,y)=2x+y-6.
$$

Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=1+\sqrt{4x-4y}.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
after.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1+2\sqrt{x-y}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=x-y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=1-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1+2\sqrt{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2\sqrt{z}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{z}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ -\int \frac{1}{2\sqrt{z}}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ -\sqrt{z} & =x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
-\sqrt{x-y}=x+C
$$

Therefore, 

$$
g(x,y)=-\sqrt{x-y}.

Question 10

Consider the differential equation dydx=1+4x−4y.

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form g(x,y)=x+C, where C is a constant. What is g(x,y)?

a
x+y
b
1x−y
c
x+yx−y
d
−1x+y
e
−x−y
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation. dydx=1+2x−y

Then, we make the substitution z=x−y. Differentiating z(x) using the chain rule, we get dzdx=1−dydx⟹dydx=1−dzdx. Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of z as follows: 1−dzdx=1+2z

Expressing this equation in the form z′(x)=f(z) gives −dzdx=2z.

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to x:

−12zdzdx=1−∫12zdz=∫dx−z=x+C

Finally, we write the equation in terms of y and x using our original substitution, as follows: −x−y=x+C

Therefore, g(x,y)=−x−y.

content.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=1+\sqrt{4x-4y}.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
content.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1+2\sqrt{x-y}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=x-y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=1-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1+2\sqrt{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2\sqrt{z}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{z}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ -\int \frac{1}{2\sqrt{z}}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ -\sqrt{z} & =x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
-\sqrt{x-y}=x+C
$$

Therefore, 

$$
g(x,y)=-\sqrt{x-y}.
$$
